title: Benefits management
blurb: Define benefits management, tell outputs, outcomes and benefits apart, and see why it runs past project closure.
question: A GP surgery's new online booking system went live on time and on budget. Six months later, the practice manager asks whether missed appointments have actually fallen as the business case promised. Which discipline answers that question, and what does it involve?

teach.body: A project delivers outputs, but the organisation invests to get benefits. Benefits management is the identification, definition, planning, tracking and realisation of benefits. In plain English: decide what improvements the project is for, how you will measure them, who will make them happen, then check they really arrive. A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome, perceived as an advantage by stakeholders.

steps.label: Output
steps.sub: What the project delivers: a new booking system

steps.label: Outcome
steps.sub: The change in use: patients book and cancel online

teach.caption: Outputs only create value when they are used. The benefit comes from the outcome, not from the output itself.

teach.h: The five activities of benefits management

steps.label: Identify
steps.sub: What improvements is the project for?

steps.label: Define
steps.sub: Describe each benefit and how it is measured

steps.label: Track
steps.sub: Monitor the measures as change takes hold

steps.label: Realise
steps.sub: Confirm the improvement has really happened

teach.caption: The order matches the definition: identification, definition, planning, tracking and realisation.

teach.body: A benefit you can't measure can't be tracked or proven. So each benefit is defined with a measure, a starting baseline, a target, an owner in the business who will make it happen, and a date when it should appear. A dis-benefit is an outcome perceived as negative by one or more stakeholders, and it is planned for and tracked too.

head: Benefit
Measure
Owner
When
teach.caption: Every benefit has a measure, an owner and a time. The dis-benefit is tracked so it can be managed, not ignored.

items.label: Benefits identified in the business case
Outputs built; benefits plan kept current
Outputs handed over to the business

teach.caption: This is why the extended life cycle adds adoption and benefits realisation after transition.

teach.body: The sponsor is accountable for benefits and for making sure they are realised, often long after the project has closed. Business owners and users realise them by adopting the change in business as usual. The project manager's job is to deliver outputs that make the benefits possible, and to keep the sponsor aware of anything that threatens them.

teach.text: Benefits management is NOT delivering the outputs on time, controlling scope changes or managing defects. It is about the VALUE: identifying, defining, planning, tracking and realising benefits. And it does not stop at handover: many benefits arrive after the project closes.

items: Benefits management: the identification, definition, planning, tracking and realisation of benefits.
A benefit is a measurable improvement from an outcome, seen as an advantage by stakeholders; a dis-benefit is seen as negative.
Output (what is delivered) → outcome (the change) → benefit (the measurable gain).
The sponsor is accountable for benefits; many are realised after the project closes.

summary: You can now define benefits management as the identification, definition, planning, tracking and realisation of benefits, and tell outputs, outcomes, benefits and dis-benefits apart. You can also explain why the sponsor stays accountable for benefits that often arrive after the project has closed.

A.q: Which of the following best defines benefits management?
options: The planning, scheduling, monitoring and control of the project's outputs
The identification, definition, planning, tracking and realisation of benefits
The capture, evaluation, approval and recording of changes to the baseline
The inspection, measurement and testing of outputs against acceptance criteria
A.why: Benefits management is the identification, definition, planning, tracking and realisation of benefits.

whyNot.0: This describes managing delivery of outputs, not the value they create.

A.q: A clinic introduces an online booking system. Which of the following is a BENEFIT rather than an output or outcome?
options: The new online booking system
Patients booking appointments online
A 25% fall in missed appointments
Training sessions for the reception team
A.why: A measurable improvement (fewer missed appointments) is a benefit; it results from the outcome of patients using the system.

whyNot.0: The system itself is an output: what the project delivers.
whyNot.1: Patients using the system is the outcome: the changed situation.
whyNot.3: Training is project work or an output, not the improvement itself.

A.q: Why does benefits management usually continue after a project has closed?
options: The project baseline has to be reset after closure
Many benefits only appear once outputs are in use
The risk register can only be closed after handover
The project team stays together to deliver benefits
A.why: Benefits come from using the outputs in business as usual, so many are realised after the project has closed.

whyNot.0: Baselines are for controlling delivery; they are not reset after closure.
whyNot.2: Risk closure happens as part of risk management, not benefits management.
whyNot.3: The temporary project team normally disbands at closure.

B.q: A warehouse automation project is being planned. Which of the following is a DIS-BENEFIT?
options: A reduction in picking errors
Installation of new conveyors
Staff using the new scanners
More noise for the neighbours
B.why: Extra noise for neighbouring residents is an outcome perceived as negative by a stakeholder group: a dis-benefit.

whyNot.0: Fewer errors is a measurable improvement: a benefit.
whyNot.1: The conveyors are an output of the project.
whyNot.2: Staff using the scanners is an outcome.

B.q: Who is accountable for making sure a project's benefits are realised?
options: The project sponsor
The project manager
The project team
The project office
B.why: The sponsor is accountable for benefits realisation, which often continues after the project closes.

whyNot.1: The PM delivers the outputs that enable benefits, but is not accountable for realising them.
whyNot.2: The team builds the outputs and usually disbands at closure.
whyNot.3: A PMO may support tracking and reporting but is not accountable.

B.q: Which sequence correctly shows how a project creates value?
options: Benefit, then output, then outcome
Outcome, then benefit, then output
Output, then benefit, then outcome
Output, then outcome, then benefit
B.why: The project delivers outputs; using them creates outcomes; outcomes produce measurable benefits.

whyNot.0: Benefits come last; they cannot exist before the output is delivered.
whyNot.1: The output must exist before anyone can use it to create an outcome.
whyNot.2: The benefit comes from the outcome, so the outcome must come first.

C.q: A new sales system was delivered on time and budget, but a year later staff still use spreadsheets and the forecast 10% sales rise has not happened. What does this show?
options: Benefits need the outputs to be adopted and used
The project failed to meet its time constraint
The benefit should be removed from the register
The project manager is accountable for the gap
C.why: Benefits come from outcomes: without adoption in business as usual the output cannot deliver the improvement.

whyNot.1: The project was on time; the problem is benefits, not schedule.
whyNot.2: Deleting the benefit hides the problem; it should be tracked and acted on.
whyNot.3: The sponsor is accountable for benefits realisation, not the PM.

C.q: Which TWO of the following are activities within benefits management? 1. Tracking benefits against their measures 2. Levelling resource usage 3. Defining how each benefit is measured 4. Auditing configuration items
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 3
C.why: Defining how benefits are measured and tracking them are both part of benefits management.

whyNot.0: Resource levelling is a scheduling and resource technique.
whyNot.1: Neither is a benefits activity: they belong to resourcing and configuration management.
whyNot.2: Auditing configuration items is part of configuration management.

C.q: Why must each benefit be defined in measurable terms?
options: So it can be added to the deployment baseline
So its realisation can be tracked and proven
So it can be transferred to a third party
So it can be delivered before handover
C.why: A benefit must be measurable so that progress can be tracked and its realisation confirmed.

whyNot.0: The deployment baseline covers delivery scope, schedule, cost and resources, not benefits tracking.
whyNot.2: Transfer is a risk response, not a reason to measure benefits.
whyNot.3: Many benefits arrive after handover, whatever their measures.

reteach.title: Think of a gym membership
reteach.question: You sign up to a gym because you want to feel fitter. What do you actually get on day one, and when does the benefit arrive?

blocks.h: The card is not the point
blocks.body: On day one you get a membership card: that's the output. Going three times a week is the outcome: a change in what you do. Running 5 km without stopping, or a lower resting heart rate, is the benefit: measurable and something you value. If the card sits in a drawer, there's no benefit. Managing the benefit means setting the target, tracking it and making sure the habit sticks.

steps.label: Dis-benefit
steps.sub: Less free time in the evening

blocks.text: Paying for the card (the output) on budget doesn't make you fitter. Projects are the same: delivering outputs is not the same as realising benefits.

explain.body: Benefits management is the identification, definition, planning, tracking and realisation of benefits. It keeps the focus on the value the project was set up to create.

test.q: Complete the statement: benefits management covers a benefit from its identification through to its ______.
options: realisation
handover
approval
baselining
test.why: Benefits management runs from identification to realisation, which often happens after handover.

whyNot.1: Handover is when outputs pass to the business; benefits are usually still to come.
whyNot.2: Approval of the business case is early in the life cycle, not the end point.
whyNot.3: Baselining relates to the delivery plan, not to benefits.

explain.body: Outputs are what the project delivers. Outcomes are the changed circumstances when people use them. Benefits are the measurable improvements that result from outcomes.

test.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between outputs and benefits?
options: Benefits are the deliverables a project creates
Benefits arise from using the project's outputs
Outputs are realised after the benefits arrive
Outputs and benefits are two names for one thing
test.why: Benefits come from the outcomes created when outputs are put to use.

whyNot.2: Outputs come first; benefits follow their use.
whyNot.3: They are different: an output is a thing, a benefit is a measurable improvement.

explain.body: A benefit is a measurable improvement perceived as an advantage by stakeholders. A dis-benefit is an outcome perceived as negative by one or more stakeholders. Both are identified, planned and tracked.

test.q: What makes an outcome a dis-benefit rather than a benefit?
options: It costs more than the budget allowed
It arrives after the project has closed
It is perceived as negative by stakeholders
It has not been measured by the project
test.why: A dis-benefit is an outcome that one or more stakeholders perceive as negative.

whyNot.0: Overspend is a cost variance, not a dis-benefit.
whyNot.1: Timing doesn't decide it; many benefits also arrive after closure.
whyNot.3: Dis-benefits should be measured too; being unmeasured doesn't define them.

explain.body: Benefits are identified in the business case and planned early, but most are realised after handover, in business as usual. The sponsor stays accountable; business owners and users make them happen.

test.q: When are most of a project's benefits typically realised?
options: During the concept phase
While outputs are being built
Once the outputs are in use
At the first decision gate
test.why: Benefits flow from using the outputs, so most are realised after handover, often after the project has closed.

whyNot.0: In concept, benefits are only identified and estimated.
whyNot.1: During the build, nothing is in use yet to create benefits.
whyNot.3: The first gate decides whether to proceed; no benefits exist yet.
